Update:

I recently had the pleasure of reading Fundamentals of General Linear Acoustics by the late Finn Jacobsen of DTU, a giant of the field, and wished I’d found it years earlier. I had read plenty of acoustics and signal processing books before, but they were vague in places, or never really connected the two. This book not only sets out the complete theory of linear acoustics as it stands today, with the equations worked out in great detail and all kinds of examples, but is also very easy to read (far easier than Theoretical Acoustics). It also introduces the relevant signal processing from an acoustics point of view, giving you a deeper understanding of both acoustics and signal processing, in theory and in practice. Several things I had only half understood became clearer after reading it.

==================

I’m in the same situation: I also moved from mechanical engineering into acoustics.

First, teaching yourself a new field takes sustained motivation. Either your project needs it, or you’re personally interested. If it’s interest, you can work through textbooks systematically from start to finish, going from the whole to the details. If it’s your project, learn as you go: look up and learn whatever you run into, branch out from one topic to the related ones you don’t know, trace things back to the fundamentals, and build out from the details to the whole. Get these the wrong way round and you’ll very likely end up wasting your effort and losing interest. So think about this question first.

Second, what exactly to read. If it’s for your project, start from the most-cited, most representative papers in your area, then go through their references and find the highly cited papers and books there, and so on. Iterate like this and you’ll end up with a sizable literature list. Get the gist of each paper first, then look up the theory you don’t understand in a targeted way.
For textbooks, I recommend the video lectures of the DSP course by MIT legend Alan Oppenheim. They’re more direct than reading a book, and you get a taste of 1970s analog style and the professor’s sexy little mustache. There’s a companion book too. It covers the most basic signal processing, from sampling to the Fourier transform to filters. One more thing: since you’ll be doing acoustics research, you also need the basics of acoustics. I recommend Acoustics by Professor Kuttruff in Germany (the former director of the institute where I did my PhD); all the basic acoustic theory is there.

Also, make full use of Google (somehow, since it’s blocked in China) to get information quickly, comprehensively and accurately.

One last thing: in research, your approach and way of thinking matter most. The specific techniques and implementation are within the intellectual reach of most graduate students; how long it takes you to learn and master them just depends on how much time and energy you put in.

For more on acoustics (popular science, curiosities, little-known facts, industrial applications and where the field is heading), see my Zhihu column Acoustics: Tech You Can Hear and my WeChat Official Account, Ziyu Acoustics.
